newsitem.title: USA: Scholars unfriendly in review of Gingrich course.
newsitem.headline: Scholars unfriendly in review of Gingrich course.

text.p: House Speaker Newt Gingrich told the House ethics committee that respected scholars reviewed and contributed to the controversial college course "Renewing American Civilisation" at the heart of his ethics travails.
What he did not say was that the reviews were bad.
The House ethics committee Friday received a scorching report by special counsel James Cole outlining a pattern of ethics violations by Gingrich and recommending a reprimand and $300,000 penalty.
At the heart of the controversy was improper use of tax-exempt charitable funds for the 40-hour course, taught by Gingrich, which the report labeled part of a partisan, political exercise.
Defending the course, Gingrich in a Dec. 8, 1994 letter stated that "respected scholars such as James Q. Wilson ... and Larry Sabato continue to contribute to and review course content."

Wilson, a professor of management and public policy at the University of California in Los Angeles and Sabato, a University of Virginia political scientist, were also referred to in a memo by individuals promoting the course.
But a footnote to the report makes it clear the academics were not overwhelmed by what Gingrich had to offer.

In a June 1993 letter to officials working with Gingrich, Wilson stated, "Perhaps I don't understand the purposes of the course, but if it is to be course rather (than) a series of sermons, this chapter won't do. It is bland, vague, hortatory, and lacking in substance."

Wilson continued, "I could go on, but I dare not for fear I have misunderstood what this enterprise is all about. I am a professor, and so I bring the perspectives (and limitations) of a professor to bear on this matter. If this is not to be a course but instead a sermon, then you should get a preacher to comment on it."

A book co-written by Sabato called "Dirty Little Secrets: The Persistence of Corruption in American Politics" said, "Nominally an educational enterprise, internal course planning documents revealed the true nature of the course as a partisan organising tool."
